# Drafting a Polite but Firm Resignation Letter from Your Job

> **In short:** A strong resignation letter is short, warm and unambiguous. It states your last day, thanks your employer, offers a smooth handover and stays professional — three short paragraphs usually do the job in under 15 minutes of writing.

**Hook:** Leaving a job is rarely just about you — it's also about the people you'll hand work to, the references you'll rely on later, and the bridges you don't want to burn. This guide walks you through writing a resignation letter that does all of that well, even if you've never resigned before.

## Before you start
- **A quiet 15–20 minutes** — that's realistically all the writing time you'll need.
- **A word processor or notes app** — Google Docs, Word, Pages, or even the Notes app on your phone.
- **Your key facts ready:** your manager's name (or "Hiring Manager" if you don't know it yet), your role title, and your planned last working day. A simple calendar helps you pick the right date.
- **Your employment contract or award nearby** — it's worth a quick check for any **notice period** (the minimum amount of time, written or implied, you have to give your employer before leaving). In Australia, the National Employment Standards set a baseline of between one and four weeks depending on how long you've been in the role. Your contract or industry award may set a longer period.
- **No special account, app, or paid tool needed** — this is plain writing.

One honest note: **a letter alone does not resign you.** In Australia, resignation is a legal act that's completed once your employer clearly understands you're ending your employment — usually a conversation plus a written record. Treat the letter as the *written record* that supports the conversation, not a substitute for it. If your workplace has a formal resignation process (an HR portal, an email template), follow that on top of the letter.

## Step 1 — Decide your last working day on a calendar
Open your calendar app or any calendar and count forward from today using your notice period. If you've been in the role for less than one year, **one week** is a common minimum; **two weeks** is the widely-expected standard in most office jobs; some industries expect four weeks or more. Pick the later of your notice period or your contract's requirement so you stay on the right side of your obligations.

💬 Example: *"Started 14 March 2024, finishing today 28 May 2026 — that's roughly two years and two months. Two weeks' notice puts my last day at Friday 13 June 2026."*

If your screen looks different, any calendar works — a paper diary, a phone calendar, or a wall planner all do the same job.

**You'll know it worked when** you can name a specific date (a weekday, not a vague "in two weeks") and you can write it at the top of your letter.

## Step 2 — Open a blank document and write the header
Create a new document and type three lines at the very top, left-aligned: **your full name**, **your email or phone**, and the **date**. Skip a line, then add the recipient's name and title (or just "Hiring Manager"), and their organisation's address. This block is what makes the letter look like an official record rather than a casual message.

If you don't have a printer-friendly format in mind, plain text with the date on its own line is perfectly fine. The point is that someone reading the letter a year from now can see who wrote it, when, and to whom.

💬 Example: *"Jane O'Connor — jane.oconnor@email.com — 28 May 2026 / Priya Shah, Head of Customer Operations, Brightline Retail Pty Ltd, Level 4, 88 Bourke Street, Melbourne VIC 3000."*

**You'll know it worked when** your document looks like a short, tidy letterhead — three lines from you, a line break, then three or four lines about the recipient.

## Step 3 — Write the opening paragraph
In one or two sentences, **state clearly that you're resigning**, **name your role**, and **give your last working day**. Don't apologise, don't over-explain, and don't hint at regret you don't feel. Clarity is a kindness — it stops your manager from having to guess what you mean.

Picture the first sentence as a doorbell: it announces you're there and what you want. Compare the two openings below:

💬 Example: *"Please accept this letter as formal notice of my resignation from my position as Customer Operations Lead at Brightline Retail. My last working day will be Friday, 13 June 2026."*

That's all paragraph one needs. Save the reasons, the thanks, and the handover offer for the next paragraphs.

**You'll know it worked when** someone reading just paragraph one could repeat back: *who* is leaving, *what* role, and *when* — without guessing.

## Step 4 — Write a short, genuine thank-you
Paragraph two is **one short paragraph** of genuine thanks — pick **one or two specific things** you appreciated. Generic praise like "great company, great team" reads as filler; a single specific detail (a mentor, a project, a learning moment) lands as sincere.

If your reasons for leaving are unhappy ones, that's okay — you can still find *one* thing worth acknowledging. It might be the training budget, a flexible-hours policy, a supportive colleague, or simply the experience itself. Avoid sounding sarcastic; future-you may need a reference from these people.

💬 Example: *"I'm grateful for the past two years, and especially for the chance to lead the 2025 service-recovery project — that experience taught me more about clear writing than anything I've done since."*

**You'll know it worked when** the paragraph sounds like something *you* would actually say to your manager in person — not a formula you copied off a website.

## Step 5 — Offer a clean handover
Paragraph three says, in plain words, **how you'll help the team after you leave**. Two or three sentences is enough: you'll write up your key tasks, brief a replacement, finish what's in progress. The aim is to leave things **better than you found them** so people remember you well.

If you don't yet know exactly what you'll hand over, that's normal — write the *intention* rather than the plan. "I'll prepare a handover document and stay available for questions" is honest and useful; "I'll make sure nothing falls over" is a promise you can keep.

💬 Example: *"Over the next two weeks I'll prepare a handover document covering my open accounts and weekly processes, and I'm happy to brief my replacement in person or by call. Please let me know who I should coordinate with so the transition is as smooth as possible for the team."*

**You'll know it worked when** your manager could read that paragraph and immediately picture what happens between today and your last day — without needing to email you for clarification.

## Step 6 — Sign off warmly and proofread
Close with a single short line wishing the team well, then sign off with "**Kind regards,**" or "**Sincerely,**" and your full name. **Read the whole letter out loud once** — this catches typos, awkward phrases, and any sentence that sounds angrier or sadder than you meant.

Look out for three things: dates that don't match the calendar, the manager's name spelled wrong, and any sentence that hints at complaints. If a sentence reads like a "burning bridges" line, soften it or cut it — even if you're tempted.

💬 Example: *"I wish the team every success going forward. Kind regards, Jane O'Connor."*

**You'll know it worked when** you can read the letter end-to-end in under a minute, it sounds like you on a calm day, and you wouldn't change a single sentence.

## Step 7 — Save, print if needed, and deliver
Save the letter as a **PDF** so the formatting stays the same on any device. If your workplace expects a printed copy, print one and sign it in pen. Most Australian workplaces accept the letter by **email** to your manager (and often HR) — ask your manager or check your employee handbook if you're unsure.

💬 Example: *"Subject: Resignation — Jane O'Connor — Customer Operations Lead. Dear Priya, Please find attached my formal resignation letter, effective end of day Friday 13 June 2026. Happy to discuss at any time that suits you. Kind regards, Jane."*

**You'll know it worked when** your manager has acknowledged the letter, your last working day is on both of your calendars, and you can stop second-guessing the wording.

## Common mistakes
- **Putting the reasons for leaving in writing.** Even if they're true, written reasons can be quoted back at you later or shared with people you didn't intend. Keep reasons for the in-person conversation; keep the letter to facts and grace.
- **Using a passive-aggressive "thank you" or fake praise.** People read tone, not just words. A line like *"Thanks for the unforgettable experience"* lands badly. If you can't think of anything nice, a simple *"I'm grateful for the opportunities I've had here"* is honest and short.
- **Forgetting to check your contract or award for the notice period.** A letter dated for two weeks' time when your award requires four can put you in breach. Always cross-check before you press send.
- **CC'ing or BCC'ing people your manager didn't expect.** Keep the first delivery simple — manager (and HR if your workplace uses it). Wider announcements are usually a conversation with your manager, not your decision alone.

## What this means for you
- **If you're leaving on good terms:** keep the letter short, warm, and focused on handover. You'll likely need a reference from these people within two years, and a graceful letter is the first step toward a strong one.
- **If you're leaving on tough terms:** keep the letter even *more* neutral. Polite, factual, future-focused. Your future self — job hunting, networking, explaining a short stint — will thank you for not putting grievances on paper.
- **If you're just getting started:** write a rough draft today, even if you're not resigning yet. Having a calm template ready means that when the day comes, you'll spend your energy on the conversation, not the wording.

## Try it now
Open a blank document and write **only** the header (Step 2) and the opening paragraph (Step 3). It should take you under three minutes. Once you see it on the page, you'll know exactly what the rest of the letter needs to do — and you can finish it whenever you're ready.
